implementation_notes: TypeScript keeps JavaScript's runtime protocol and types it: a class implements Iterable<T> by declaring [Symbol.iterator](): Iterator<T>, for...of then checks the element type, and the standard library declarations (lib.es2015.iterable.d.ts) supply the same interfaces for Array, Map, Set and String. When compiling to ES5 the downlevelIteration compiler option decides what the emitted loop does - without it, for...of is translated to an index loop and objects that only implement Symbol.iterator throw at runtime; spread and destructuring are affected by the same flag. Exposing enumeration on a type therefore means exposing Iterable<T> (or IterableIterator<T>) and keeping the backing store private.
pitfalls: With a target below ES2015 and no downlevelIteration, for...of over an object that only implements Symbol.iterator is emitted as an index-based loop and fails at runtime ('Object is not iterable').

The declarations are erased: TypeScript does not verify that a class claiming Iterable<T> actually behaves as one, so a wrong or missing iterator implementation compiles and fails only when the loop runs.

Iterating a Map or Set with for...of is fine, but iterating a plain object literal is not - Object.entries/Object.keys must be inserted, and their element types (unknown[] for entries) should be narrowed rather than cast with any.
